The glass caught the last light of dusk like a trapped sun. Maren pulled it from the tide pool, fingers trembling against the salt-crusted cork. Inside, a slip of paper bore her own handwriting.

*You will forget. The light must not go out.*

She laughed—a hollow sound swallowed by wind. A prank, surely. Someone on the mainland with too much time and a cruel sense of humor. She tucked the bottle back into her coat pocket and climbed the spiral stairs to begin her shift.

By midnight, the flame held steady. By two, the fog rolled in thick and gray, pressing against the windows like something wanting in. Maren checked the logbook as she always did—date, weather, fuel remaining. Her pen stopped mid-sentence.

The last entry was hers. November 12th. *Fog rolled in. Burned the wick to nothing. Forgot to check the oil.*

Her hands went cold. She had no memory of writing it. She reached into her pocket and drew the bottle out again, and in the dim amber glow, she read the words once more.

*You will forget.*

Maren looked at the flame, then at the empty reservoir beneath it, and understood at last what the sea had returned to her.
